## Exercise 5.1

I understand that in computer graphics, to process milions of RGB pairs with high frame-per-second, each pixel must be calculated parallely.  
The way we describe and define shape, line in shaders reflects this notion.

I implemented piet painting by interpreting there is 5 x 6 grids, and based on the position color is changing.

```c++
#ifdef GL_ES
precision mediump float;
#endif

uniform vec2 u_resolution;

void main() {
    vec2 uv = gl_FragCoord.xy / u_resolution.xy;

    float vertical[4];
    vertical[0] = 0.146;
    vertical[1] = 0.382;
    vertical[2] = 0.618;
    vertical[3] = 0.854;

    float horizontal[5];
    horizontal[0] = 0.090;
    horizontal[1] = 0.236;
    horizontal[2] = 0.500;
    horizontal[3] = 0.764;
    horizontal[4] = 0.910;

    int column = 0;
    int row = 0;
    float lineWidth = 0.008;
    float gridLine = 0.0;

    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
        if (uv.x > vertical[i]) column++;
        if (abs(uv.x - vertical[i]) < lineWidth) gridLine = 1.0;
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        if (uv.y < horizontal[i]) row++;
        if (abs(uv.y - horizontal[i]) < lineWidth) gridLine = 1.0;
    }

    vec3 color = vec3(0.94, 0.92, 0.84);

    if ((row == 1 || row == 2) &&
        (column == 1 || column == 2)) {
        color = vec3(0.80, 0.05, 0.04);
    }

    if ((row == 0 || row == 1) && column == 3 ||
        (row == 4 || row == 5) && column == 0) {
        color = vec3(0.95, 0.75, 0.05);
    }

    if ((row == 4 || row == 5) && column == 3) {
        color = vec3(0.03, 0.20, 0.55);
    }

    if ((row == 3 || row == 4) &&
        (column == 1)) {
        color = vec3(0.02);
    }

    if (gridLine > 0.5) color = vec3(0.02);

    if ((abs(uv.x - vertical[1]) < lineWidth &&
         uv.y > horizontal[2] && uv.y < horizontal[4]) ||
        (abs(uv.y - horizontal[3]) < lineWidth &&
         uv.x > vertical[0] && uv.x < vertical[2])) {
        color = vec3(0.80, 0.05, 0.04);
    }

    if (abs(uv.y - horizontal[0]) < lineWidth &&
        uv.x > vertical[2] && uv.x < vertical[3]) {
        color = vec3(0.03, 0.20, 0.55);
    }

    gl_FragColor = vec4(color, 1.0);
}

```

And this is the result:
![Shader result](Screenshot%202026-10-02%20at%2018.02.53.png)

And the ground truth is:
![Piet Mondrian reference](Screenshot%202026-10-02%20at%2018.05.31.png)

And I am more curious of why this shader's "grammar"(or code design?) ensure that parallelization.
My understanding is that there are two key ideas:
1. Each time main() runs, it has its own local variables, means independent. One run does not read or modify another run’s working state.
2. Just provideing the coordinates of the fragment being processed to the main() using `gl_FragCoord`, so the same code can compute colors for different locations parallelly.



## Exercise 5.2
I was inspired by [this artwork](https://www.shadertoy.com/view/MlyBWh) on Shadertoy.
In this work, the zooming target is the center and doesn't move.  I wanted to move it while continuing to see a repeating, more complex shape.
I used genAI a lot, but I thought about the overall design of the code by myself.

First, I needed to make the pattern, which has the same pattern(or copy) everywhere, because we are zooming up towards the random coordinates, so the pattern should be everywhere.
I chose the Sierpiński triangle pattern: a triangle divided into three smaller triangles, which you will see.

The core idea to implement this pattern is changing the point's coordinates so that the smaller triangle becomes the same size and position as the original triangle. 

```c++
p = 2.0 * p - corner;
```
Multiplying by 2.0 scales the smaller triangle up to the original size. Subtracting corner moves it into the original position. This lets us apply the same pattern rule again in the next loop.


Then, to understand how to implement the zoom, I examined the original code:

```c++
float z = mix(1.0, 1.0 / phiToThe4th, u);
vec2 q = uv * z;
```

Here, z changes over time and scales the coordinates used to sample the pattern. As z decreases, a smaller region of the pattern fills the screen, creating a zoom-in effect.

I kept this structure and added circular movement:

```c++
vec2 center = mix(currentCenter, nextCenter, progress);
vec2 q = uv * z + center;
```
Here, I added a randomly selected zoom target. Adding `center` to the scaled coordinates changes which part of the pattern the view zooms into.

Then the final code is 
```c++
const float SQRT3 = 1.73205080757;

float randomChoice(float seed)
{
    return fract(sin(seed * 127.1 + 311.7) * 43758.5453);
}

float cross2(vec2 a, vec2 b)
{
    return a.x * b.y - a.y * b.x;
}

float segmentDistance(vec2 p, vec2 a, vec2 b)
{
    vec2 edge = b - a;
    float t = clamp(
        dot(p - a, edge) / dot(edge, edge),
        0.0, 1.0
    );

    return length(p - a - edge * t);
}

float triangleDistance(vec2 p, vec2 a, vec2 b, vec2 c)
{
    float d = min(
        segmentDistance(p, a, b),
        min(
            segmentDistance(p, b, c),
            segmentDistance(p, c, a)
        )
    );

    bool inside =
        cross2(b - a, p - a) >= 0.0 &&
        cross2(c - b, p - b) >= 0.0 &&
        cross2(a - c, p - c) >= 0.0;

    return inside ? -d : d;
}

float triforceDistance(vec2 p)
{
    vec2 a = vec2(-0.5, 0.0);
    vec2 b = vec2( 0.5, 0.0);
    vec2 c = vec2( 0.0, SQRT3 * 0.5);

    float d = triangleDistance(p, a, b, c);
    float scale = 1.0;

    for (int i = 0; i < 18; i++)
    {
        vec2 ab = (a + b) * 0.5;
        vec2 bc = (b + c) * 0.5;
        vec2 ca = (c + a) * 0.5;

        float hole = triangleDistance(p, ab, bc, ca);
        d = max(d, -hole / scale);

        vec2 corner;

        if (p.y >= SQRT3 * 0.25)
            corner = c;
        else if (p.x < 0.0)
            corner = a;
        else
            corner = b;

        p = 2.0 * p - corner;
        scale *= 2.0;
    }

    return d;
}

void mainImage(out vec4 fragColor, in vec2 fragCoord)
{
    vec2 uv = (fragCoord - 0.5 * iResolution.xy)
            / min(iResolution.x, iResolution.y);

    // Choose a new destination every three seconds.
    float stageTime = iTime / 3.0;
    float cycle = floor(stageTime / 12.0);
    float stage = mod(stageTime, 12.0);
    int step = int(floor(stage));

    float progress = smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, fract(stage));

    vec2 a = vec2(-0.5, 0.0);
    vec2 b = vec2( 0.5, 0.0);
    vec2 c = vec2( 0.0, SQRT3 * 0.5);
    vec2 triangleCenter = (a + b + c) / 3.0;

    vec2 offset = vec2(0.0);
    float size = 1.0;

    // Follow the previously selected smaller triangles.
    for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++)
    {
        if (i >= step)
            break;

        float choice = floor(
            3.0 * randomChoice(float(i) + cycle * 37.0)
        );

        vec2 corner = choice < 1.0 ? a
                    : choice < 2.0 ? b : c;

        offset += size * 0.5 * corner;
        size *= 0.5;
    }

    // Select the next smaller triangle.
    float choice = floor(
        3.0 * randomChoice(float(step) + cycle * 37.0)
    );

    vec2 corner = choice < 1.0 ? a
                : choice < 2.0 ? b : c;

    vec2 currentCenter = offset + size * triangleCenter;
    vec2 nextCenter = offset
                    + size * 0.5 * corner
                    + size * 0.5 * triangleCenter;

    vec2 center = mix(currentCenter, nextCenter, progress);

    float z = size * pow(0.5, progress);
    vec2 q = uv * z + center;

    float d = triforceDistance(q) / z;
    float aa = max(
        fwidth(d),
        1.0 / min(iResolution.x, iResolution.y)
    );

    float fill = 1.0 - smoothstep(-aa, aa, d);

    vec3 background = vec3(0.025, 0.035, 0.045);
    vec3 gold = vec3(1.0, 0.76, 0.16);

    fragColor = vec4(mix(background, gold, fill), 1.0);
}
```
